title: Researchers explore the use of AI and smart sensors to improve food safety quickly, affordably
excerpt: The smartJAN project, developed by the eVIDA research group at the University of Deusto in collaboration with Kernet and Fundación Miranda, has completed the development of a functional prototype capable of detecting the presence of LTPs (lipid transfer proteins), a family of plant proteins that includes allergens capable of triggering severe allergic reactions. These allergens are particularly relevant in the Mediterranean region.
content_html:
The smartJAN project, developed by the eVIDA research group at the University of Deusto in collaboration with Kernet and Fundación Miranda, has completed the development of a functional prototype capable of detecting the presence of LTPs (lipid transfer proteins), a family of plant proteins that includes allergens capable of triggering severe allergic reactions. These allergens are particularly relevant in the Mediterranean region.

The initiative combines near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) with signal-processing algorithms and artificial intelligence. The technology works by shining light onto the food and analyzing how it is reflected. This produces a spectral 'fingerprint' which the artificial intelligence system interprets instantly to determine whether the product contains potentially harmful substances, without the need to destroy it or send it to a laboratory.

The work is published in the journal Food Analytical Methods.

From university research to the food industry

The main aim of the research was to test the technical feasibility of detecting allergenic proteins from the LTP family, which are found in many plant-based foods. These include Pru p 3, found mainly in peach skin, and Ara h 9, found in peanuts, both of which were studied as part of the project.

Begoña García-Zapirain, head of Deusto's eVIDA research group, points out that the technology could have a much wider range of applications. Previous tests have demonstrated its effectiveness in detecting gluten and the presence of bacteria in meat. The system could therefore also pave the way for the early detection of pathogens that cause food poisoning, such as Salmonella.

Following the completion of the initial phase and the development of a validated prototype, the project is now ready to move toward commercialization. The device is not intended for end consumers or domestic use, but rather for integration into quality control processes in the food industry, distribution chains and institutional catering facilities.

Once the protocols for validating its reliability have been completed, the speed of the analysis could facilitate food screening and complement conventional analytical methods, helping to speed up quality control procedures and strengthen food safety.

Vulnerable groups

The participation of Fundación Miranda in the consortium adds a social dimension focused on health care for people over 65, a group for whom the prevention of food-related risks and attention to specific dietary needs are particularly important.

With the research phase now complete, the next step toward bringing this tool to market will depend on industrial interest in turning the prototype into a commercially available testing device.
